subject: Environment
description: Solar, wind, nuclear, hydroelectric — India's capacity

questions.stem: Which of the following is a RENEWABLE source of energy?

options.option_text: Coal
Solar
Natural gas
Petroleum

questions.explanation: Renewable: solar, wind, hydro, geothermal, tidal, biomass (sustainably used). Non-renewable: fossil fuels (coal, oil, gas), uranium. Solar energy = effectively unlimited for practical lifetimes.
questions.subject: Environment

questions.stem: India's largest SOLAR PARK (as of 2024) is at:

options.option_text: Kurnool (Andhra Pradesh)
Bhadla Solar Park (Rajasthan)
Pavagada (Karnataka)
Charanka (Gujarat)

questions.explanation: Bhadla Solar Park (Jodhpur, Rajasthan) — capacity ~2,245 MW, world's largest solar park by area at one point (~14,000 acres). Pavagada is second (~2,050 MW). Khavda (Gujarat) is the LARGEST under-development renewable park (30 GW target).
questions.subject: Environment

questions.stem: India's TARGET for installed non-fossil-fuel capacity by 2030 (as per the 2021 Glasgow commitment / Panchamrit) is:

options.option_text: 100 GW
500 GW
250 GW

questions.explanation: 500 GW non-fossil-fuel capacity by 2030 — part of India's COP26 'Panchamrit'. Also: 50% of electricity from renewables by 2030; reduce carbon intensity of economy by 45% (from 2005 levels); reduce 1 billion tonnes total emissions; net-zero by 2070.
questions.subject: Environment

questions.stem: Match the STATE with its RENEWABLE-energy strength. A. Tamil Nadu.  B. Gujarat.  C. Andhra Pradesh.  D. Karnataka. List-II: 1. Wind (largest capacity historically).  2. Solar (Khavda, Charanka).  3. Solar + wind (Kurnool, Anantapur).  4. Solar (Pavagada).
questions.explanation: TN — historically leads wind (Kanyakumari, Tirunelveli). Gujarat — solar + wind leader (Khavda hybrid park, Charanka); also world's largest offshore-wind potential. AP — Kurnool Ultra-Mega Solar Park, Anantapur. Karnataka — Pavagada Solar Park.

questions.stem: India's first NUCLEAR power reactor was commissioned at:

options.option_text: Kakrapar (Gujarat)
Tarapur (Maharashtra, 1969)
Kudankulam (Tamil Nadu)
Rawatbhata (Rajasthan)

questions.explanation: Tarapur Atomic Power Station — Units 1 and 2 (Boiling Water Reactors, BWR) commissioned 1969 — India's first. Built with US collaboration (General Electric). Now NPCIL (Nuclear Power Corporation of India Ltd) operates it.

questions.stem: The PRINCIPLE of HYDROELECTRIC power generation is:

options.option_text: Chemical reactions release energy
Gravitational potential of water converted into kinetic then electrical energy via turbines
Evaporation drives a heat engine
Splitting of water molecules

questions.explanation: Dam creates head (height difference). Water flows down through turbines, driving generators. No fuel, no emissions during operation. Tehri (Uttarakhand), Bhakra Nangal (Punjab/HP), Sardar Sarovar (Gujarat), Koyna (Maharashtra) — major Indian hydroelectric projects.

questions.stem: 'International Solar Alliance' (ISA) founder member nations are:

options.option_text: India + Germany
India + France
India + China
India + UK

questions.explanation: ISA — co-founded by PM Modi + French President François Hollande at COP21 (Paris, Nov 2015). HQ at NISE campus, Gurugram, India. Focus on solar deployment in 121 'Sunshine Countries' between Tropics of Cancer & Capricorn.

questions.stem: A biogas plant digests cattle dung and agricultural waste. Which gas constitutes the primary combustible component of the raw biogas produced?

options.option_text: Methane (CH₄), which constitutes 55–65% of raw biogas output
Carbon dioxide (CO₂), which makes up 35–45% of biogas by volume
Hydrogen sulphide (H₂S), responsible for the foul odour in biogas
Nitrogen gas (N₂), released during aerobic breakdown of cattle dung

questions.explanation: Methane (CH₄) is the combustible energy carrier in biogas, comprising 55–65% by volume; it is this fraction that burns to produce heat or electricity. CO₂ (35–45%) is the other major component but is non-combustible. H₂S is only a trace impurity (< 1%) and is actually removed before use.

questions.stem: PM-KUSUM (Kisan Urja Suraksha evam Utthaan Mahabhiyan) scheme was launched to deploy solar energy primarily for which beneficiary group?

options.option_text: Heavy manufacturing industries seeking to cut electricity costs
Urban rooftop households under the PM Surya Ghar solar scheme
Farmers — for solarising pumps and grid-connected rural plants
Railway traction yards requiring stable uninterrupted power supply

questions.explanation: PM-KUSUM targets the agricultural sector: it subsidises solar-powered irrigation pumps and supports small grid-connected solar plants on barren/fallow farmland. PM Surya Ghar (launched 2024) is the separate urban rooftop scheme — a common exam-trap distractor. Railways and industries have their own renewable schemes.

questions.stem: Which of the following geothermal sites in India has surface spring temperatures exceeding 80°C and is recognised as the country's highest-potential geothermal energy field?

options.option_text: Tattapani (Chhattisgarh) — explored by ONGC for deep drilling
Manikaran (Himachal Pradesh) — sacred hot-spring pilgrimage site
Puga Valley (Ladakh) — boiling springs exceeding 84°C at surface
Taptapani (Odisha) — moderate therapeutic spring tourist cluster

questions.explanation: Puga Valley in Ladakh has India's most promising geothermal resource, with surface temperatures above 84°C and evidence of steam and sulphur fields. Manikaran (HP) is famous but lower in energy potential; Tattapani (CG) is under ONGC exploration at much lower temperatures; Taptapani (Odisha) is only a therapeutic spring.

questions.stem: India's National Green Hydrogen Mission, approved in January 2023, has set a domestic production target of how many million metric tonnes (MMT) per annum of green hydrogen by 2030?

options.option_text: 2 million metric tonnes per annum — revised MNRE conservative goal
10 million metric tonnes per annum — aspirational Paris-linked aim
7 million metric tonnes per annum — NITI Aayog interim projection
5 million metric tonnes per annum — official NGHM target by 2030

questions.explanation: The National Green Hydrogen Mission (January 2023) officially targets 5 MMT per annum production by 2030, with an outlay of ₹19,744 crore and projected investment of ₹8 lakh crore. The 10 MMT figure circulates as an aspirational ceiling but is not the official Cabinet-approved target. 2 MMT and 7 MMT are distractors.

questions.stem: The 'Plant Load Factor' (PLF) is a performance metric used for power stations. Which of the following definitions correctly describes PLF?

options.option_text: Efficiency of turbines measured in British Thermal Units per hour
Ratio of actual units generated to maximum possible in a time period
Ratio of coal consumed to total calorific value of fuel at the plant
Ratio of installed capacity to peak demand served on the power grid

questions.explanation: PLF = (Actual energy generated ÷ Maximum possible energy if running at rated capacity throughout the period) × 100%. Indian thermal plants typically average 55–60% PLF. Option D describes a capacity-utilisation or reserve-margin concept; Option C describes heat-rate efficiency, not PLF. PLF is the primary utilisation metric cited in CEA reports.

questions.stem: Which international body publishes the annual 'Renewable Power Generation Costs' report that tracks the Levelized Cost of Energy (LCOE) for solar, wind, and other renewables globally?

options.option_text: IEA (International Energy Agency), headquartered in Paris, France
UNEP (United Nations Environment Programme), secretariat in Nairobi
WEC (World Energy Council) — global multi-energy policy body, London
IRENA (International Renewable Energy Agency), based in Abu Dhabi

questions.explanation: IRENA, headquartered at Masdar City, Abu Dhabi (UAE), publishes the annual 'Renewable Power Generation Costs' report — the globally cited reference for LCOE trends. India is a founding member (2009). The IEA (Paris) publishes the World Energy Outlook and tracks broader energy data but is not the author of this specific report. UNEP and WEC do not publish LCOE cost-tracking reports.

questions.stem: Section 86(1)(e) of the Electricity Act, 2003 empowers State Electricity Regulatory Commissions to mandate that distribution licensees purchase a minimum percentage of electricity from renewable sources. What is this statutory instrument called?

options.option_text: Green Energy Open Access (GEOA) — Ministry of Power Rule 2022
Carbon Credit Exchange (CCX) — UNFCCC-linked emissions trading unit
Renewable Purchase Obligation (RPO) — statutory RE procurement quota
Perform Achieve and Trade (PAT) — Bureau of Energy Efficiency scheme

questions.explanation: Renewable Purchase Obligation (RPO) under Section 86(1)(e) of the Electricity Act, 2003 compels distribution companies to source a set percentage of total electricity from renewables; SERCs specify state-wise targets (e.g., 43% by 2030 as per recent MoP trajectory). PAT (Perform Achieve Trade) is an energy-efficiency scheme under BEE, not a renewable quota. GEOA (2022) governs open-access rights for consumers, not utility procurement mandates.
